name: Côte d'Ivoire
summary_text: Consensual same-sex sexual acts between adults in private are legal in Côte d'Ivoire and have never been criminalized.  Article 360 of the Penal Code punishes public breach of decency with three months to two years imprisonment and a fine of 50,000 to 500,000 francs. Where the breach consists of an indecent or contrary-to-nature act with an individual of the same sex, the penalty is six months to two years imprisonment and a fine of 50,000 to 300,000 francs, doubled if committed against a minor or in the presence of a minor of eighteen years.  Under Articles 358 and 359 the age of consent is 18 for homosexual couples and 15 for heterosexual couples.  Côte d'Ivoire provides no legal protection against discrimination based on gender identity. No legal protection against discrimination based on sexual orientation exists either.  The government does not recognize same-sex couples.  The United States Department of State 2023 report on human rights practices records three deaths within the LGBTQI+ community during that year. In the same year a transgender man was beaten in Abobo, a district of Abidjan, while walking with another man. Police responses to such non-state violence were sometimes slow and ineffective and often blamed the victim, although authorities were handling complaints somewhat better than in previous years. Many victims do not report to police because they believe they will not be taken seriously.  In September and October 2024, 45 assault incidents were recorded in Abidjan. Social media influencers called for violence during that period. A homophobia-motivated attack occurred at a market employing gay hair stylists. After these attacks people avoided going out during the day and meeting publicly and remained hypervigilant.  Transgender women and other feminine-presenting people assigned male at birth face an especially high risk of violence because their gender expression breaks social norms and draws hostile attention. Peer-reviewed research published in 2015 found that travestis, people born anatomically male who live as women, face harsher stigmatization and violence than sexual minorities whose gender normativity avoids attention.  During the 2010-2011 post-electoral crisis, the Force Républicaines de Côte d’Ivoire beat and abused gay men and transgender persons, most of them sex workers. Complaints were not filed for fear of reprisals. Fighters were more aggressive toward transvestis, defined as transgender and otherwise gender non-conforming people assigned male at birth. In 2012 members of the same force repeatedly raided Le Club, a bar in Abidjan frequented by gender and sexual minorities, mainly targeting effeminate men and transvestis, forcing them into a cargo truck, sometimes forcing them to remove clothes, and demanding a significant fine under threat of being taken to bases.  In September 2024 the National Human Rights Council called on the public to refrain from online hatred and violence toward woubis, gay men and trans women, and lelés, lesbians and trans men, stating that despite their different sexual orientation and contrary to customs and traditions, members of this woubi community remain human beings and benefit from human rights enshrined in the Ivorian Constitution and international human rights treaties. In 2024 President Ouattara promised to introduce a bill to Parliament to counter the expansion of homosexuality.  Discrimination in healthcare continues, including refusal of care on grounds of sexual orientation.

sources.title: U.S. Department of State - 2011 Human Rights Report (Côte d'Ivoire)
sources.documents: Widespread societal stigmatization; government failure to counter it; beatings, imprisonment, verbal abuse, humiliation, extortion of gay men by police/gendarmes/armed forces; FRCI beating/abuse of gay men and transgender persons, mostly sex workers; complaints not filed for fear of reprisals; precarious post-electoral crisis situation.

name: Cameroon
summary_text: Article 347-1 of the penal code in Cameroon criminalises both male and female same-sex sexual activity and carries up to five years' imprisonment. The first penal code enacted in 1965 did not criminalise consensual same-sex acts. An ordinance issued in September 1972 by President Ahmadou Ahidjo introduced Article 347bis, now numbered 347-1. The 2016 penal code explicitly outlawed same-sex relations. Under the earlier provision sentences ran between six months and five years.  In Douala on 8 February 2021, two transgender women, Shakiro and Patricia, were arrested in a restaurant for wearing women's clothing. Shakiro, born 29 July 1997 in Douala, had built a Facebook and YouTube following discussing trans life. Both women were convicted of attempted homosexuality, public indecency and failing to carry identification. Each received five years' imprisonment plus a fine of 200,000 CFA francs ($370), the maximum statutory term. They had been detained since February 2021 and spent five months in prison before a judge ordered release pending appeal. An appeal was filed. Defence lawyers Alice Nkom and Richard Tamfu described the verdict as a political decision with no proof of acts. Shakiro subsequently fled Cameroon to claim asylum abroad.  Gender presentation alone has supported convictions in earlier cases. In November 2011 Jonas Kimie and Franky Ndome were sentenced to five years after arrest outside a nightclub. The trial judge treated manner of speech, wearing women's clothing and ordering a cream-based liquor as sufficient evidence of homosexuality. No sexual act was observed. An appeals court acquitted both men on 9 January 2013.  Enforcement extends beyond presentation cases. In 2011 at least a dozen men were detained under Section 347. Jean-Claude Roger Mbede was sentenced to three years at Kondengui Central Prison for sending SMS messages to a male acquaintance. On 24 November 2011 three young men were sentenced to five years for oral sex in a parked car. In May 2005 eleven men were arrested at a nightclub on suspicion of sodomy. Authorities threatened medical examinations to prove activity. The men remained detained into February 2006, with trials scheduled for March 2006 and release in April 2006.  Human Rights Watch documented an uptick of violence in 2022. Since 9 March of that year security forces arbitrarily arrested at least six people and detained eleven people, all victims of group attacks, for alleged consensual same-sex conduct and gender nonconformity. Gendarmes beat two detainees. The organisation found that the criminalisation law enables abuse by civilians and security forces without consequence, a finding attributed to senior researcher Ilaria Allegrozzi. Beatings of gay and trans people in public are reported as common.  Law No. 2010/012 of 21 December 2010 on Cybersecurity and Cybercrime further punishes same-sex propositioning online. Article 83(1) punishes sexual propositions to a person of the same sex through electronic communications with one to two years' imprisonment and a fine of 500,000 to 1,000,000 CFA francs, or one of those penalties. Article 83(2) doubles the penalty where intercourse followed.  Failure to carry identification was charged alongside the anti-homosexuality counts against Shakiro and Patricia. Prison conditions pose an additional risk. Prisoners accused of homosexuality describe the main prison in Douala as hell.
